OpenAI shared a repository of mathematical results obtained by an internal AI model today. Here is a list of the results. Perhaps surprisingly, there are several results in category theory included.

The ones I spotted from skimming through:

  • Fiber functors for finite symmetric tensor categories in positive characteristic
  • Thomason Model Structures in Every Strict Higher Dimension
  • The Grothendieck homotopy hypothesis via elementary expansions
(I'm drawing attention to these only because I think it's wise to keep abreast of the progress of computer-assisted mathematics in one's own field, not because I endorse this practice.)
The first one of these was actually done mere days ago: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04096, posted by Kevin Coulembier and Johannes Flake

The main ideas in the proofs in Section 3 and Section 4 were originally obtained using
GPT-6 Astra, using as an input the formula in Equation (1.1), which was obtained previously using
extensive numerical experiments with the help of Claude 4.6–5 Opus.
And the OpenAI document doesn't cite them.

And the OpenAI document doesn't cite them.

I would guess OpenAI obtained the result some time ago, generated a PDF, and then didn't update the PDF in the meantime to take into account any new results.
But it sounds like the result was proven by ChatGPT either way; the only real difference was who wrote up the proof.
God I didn't expect to be so disgusted by reading the repo. It's like seeing a forest being razed.
They just dumped 300+ problems?
Looks like they really took the advice from our colleagues seriously... :grimacing:

They announced some time ago they had obtained this number of results and apparently consulted with some members of the mathematical community about the best way to proceed, so presumably there was a sufficiently significant number of people calling for this approach.

I sent this message to the authors of the new york times article on this subject:

Hello Kenneth and Siobhan,
Regarding your NYT article which was published today:
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/06/science/openai-math-problems.html
I am a category theorist and I would like to draw your attention to one of the problems that was claimed to be solved:
https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/Fiber-functors-for-finite-symmetric-tensor-categories-in-positive-characteristic-September-24-2026/paper.pdf
The same result appears to recently have published on the arxiv preprint server, and openai do not cite the original authors:
https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04096
This was brought to my attention by my colleague Dr. David Michael Roberts on the category theory zulip server:
https://categorytheory.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/241990-community.3A-discussion/topic/OpenAI.20preprint.20release/with/629770853
Here is an invite link to the forum which he raised this concern:
https://categorytheory.zulipchat.com/join/XXXXXXX
I would encourage you to contact the original authors, as they could have discussed their ideas with an openai model.
This is particularly concerning to myself and other mathematicians.  This gives credence to Prof. Tristan Buckmaster who claimed that openai plagiarised his work in the openai announcement regarding the Navier-Stokes conjecture:
https://cims.nyu.edu/%7Etristanb/statement.pdf
Kind regards,
Dr. Cole Comfort

@David Michael Roberts

In retrospect, I should have asked if you would want me to send this message to journalists.
But I think it is important that the press consult experts when discussing this subject.
@Cole Comfort not a problem. If the NYT wants to interview or mention me or whatever I don't mind. But really they should talk to Kevin C

Even supposing that were the case, one might wonder to what extent the mathematicians have only themselves to blame. The AI companies don't try very hard to hide their attitude towards copyright, attribution, etc.

I do not cast blame on mathematicians for discussions which they may have had with ai models. It is the standard practice in mathematics that the result of private discussions can not be published independently without appropriate acknowledgement. I don't see the ethical difference between an individual or company breaking this rule.
There isn't an ethical difference. But OpenAI have proven themselves time and time again to be an unethical company.

Maybe it is a good idea for users of openai products to disable the following setting:
Improve the model for everyone

Thibaut Benjamin chimed in to clarify

I was made aware I was cited on this, so let me clarify my position, which I think has been slightly exaggerated here :)

  • All this is all based on early impressions, at the time I am still processing what's in the paper (and even more so this morning)
  • As far as I can tell, the proof strategy is roughly the same everyone I know who's thought of the problem has been trying (myself included)
  • I think Prop 4.3 is where the real meat is. It's a problem that I know to be hard and technical (combinatorial) and I cannot yet understand the provided proof. What I can say is that said proof seems far below the combinatorial complexity I would expect, which I find suspect.
  • I was made aware since this morning that there is a Lean artefact accompanying this paper. Early work by my colleagues seems to indicate that the lean result indeed corresponds to the claimed result in the paper.

https://mathstodon.xyz/@thiben/117400709229046075

Many of these results were not yet verified using Lean, so some are being withdrawn:

In “Algebraicity of Weil classes on split abelian eightfolds” a sign error invalidates a stabilization-trace cancellation argument and the construction used by two dependent papers. As a result, we have withdrawn the following three manuscripts:

  • Algebraicity of Weil classes on split abelian eightfolds
  • Algebraicity of Kuga–Satake Correspondences for K3 Surfaces
  • The rational Hodge conjecture for products of K3 surfaces

The withdrawn papers now carry notices explaining the gap and linking to the archived manuscripts.

Others are being corrected.
Imagining the people doing the correcting brings to mind the people that work to collect plastic bottles on huge heaps of imported trash, trying to recover value from mass-produced garbage.

Here's an intriguing paper on the arXiv:

  • Alexander Bastounis, Fabian Circelli and Anders C. Hansen, Navier-Stokes lost in translation: Why Lean verification of AI autoformalisation does not guarantee correct natural language proofs.

I haven't verified this paper, but here's part of what it says:

It is natural to ask whether this formalisation in Lean represents a semantically faithful translation of the NL [natural language] paper, so that we can conclude that the NL paper represents a correct proof? Interestingly, OpenAI’s announced proof becomes a great source for examples of mistranslations, exactly as pointed out in §2. In particular, the Lean formalisation does not represent a semantically faithful translation of the NL paper, meaning that the Lean formalisation provides no guarantee that the NL proof is correct. We provide several examples below.
I think the claim is not that the Lean-verified proof is not really a proof of Navier-Stokes, just that the proof you can read in English has mistakes.

This was posted on 7 October. Also in there:

Statement on AI Use
The original idea of applying Chai’s rigidity results to the Hovey–Strickland conjecture arose
from the author’s work on questions related to Shimura varieties. In that context, the author
had become familiar with Chai’s methods for studying invariant formal subvarieties and density
phenomena. This led the author to consider whether these methods could be applied to the
action of the Morava stabilizer group on Lubin–Tate deformation spaces, and thereby to the
Hovey–Strickland conjecture.
The main conceptual route originated from the author’s observation described above. After the
proof of the general statement was formulated, ChatGPT was used on September 8, 2026 to check
that the author’s method works in height-3 case. AI assistance was subsequently used for proof
auditing. On September 10, 2026, during a review of the argument, ChatGPT identified a problem
in the original proof of theorem 6.1 concerning the passage from infinite Cartier-coordinate data
to finite jets. It suggested the fixed-jet repair developed in Appendix A. The resulting argument
was then rewritten, checked, and incorporated into the proof by the author. This is the only part
of the proof whose initial argument was generated by AI.

@Ivan Di Liberti One should give a disclaimer here: opting out is useful, but also the wording is seriously misleading and can create a false sense of security.

These opt-outs don't opt out from OpenAI using your content to improve and develop their services and conduct research. Conducting research is of course a maximally broad, and very relevant mandate. All uses that aren't literally training a model (evals, benchmarking, distillation, etc.) remain authorized with the toggle off. The mathematical substance of your sessions can still lawfully flow into OpenAI's internal work through research, evaluation, de-identified reuse, or human review all without violating the policy as written.

It's easy to do things that can recreate the pattern observed in the OpenAI release even if they haven't literally trained on the data.

For example, if I build an evaluation set from your sessions and test internal models against it ("I wonder, can our new model improve upon incomplete proofs or partial results written by an older model?"), that's not training on your data. But the resulting proofs will very much be followup work from user content.
